bib.title: CatBoost: unbiased boosting with categorical features

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "CatBoost: unbiased boosting with categorical features", Prokhorenkova, Gusev, Vorobev, Dorogush, Gulin (Yandex/MIPT). This PDF is arXiv:1706.09516v5, dated 20 Jan 2019, and its footer reads "Preprint. Work in progress." It prints no venue, so the NeurIPS 2018 citation in note 07 cannot be confirmed from this file.

COVERAGE: 70,940 of 70,940 chars, including Appendices A-G. Nothing was skipped. References were skimmed for origins. The proof algebra in Appendix A was read but is garbled (see PROBLEMS).

CLAIMS

- claim: CatBoost in its strong setting beats LightGBM and XGBoost on all nine datasets, and the gaps range from negligible to large.
  number: Adult +2.4% and +2.2% logloss; Amazon +17% for both; Internet +6.8% and +7.9%; Upselling +0.3% and +0.04%
  setup: Binary tasks; random 80/20 split; 5-fold CV for tuning; 50 steps of Hyperopt TPE minimising logloss; then a tree-count search over [1, 5000]. Epsilon used default parameters and tuned tree count only. Baselines received ordered TS as a preprocessing step. CatBoost ran in Ordered mode with feature combinations. Versions: catboost 0.3, xgboost 0.6, lightgbm 0.1.
  quote: "Adult 0.270 / 0.127 +2.4% / +1.9% +2.2% / +1.0%" and "Amazon 0.139 / 0.044 +17% / +21% +17% / +21%" and "Upselling 0.166 / 0.049 +0.3% / +0.1% +0.04% / +0.3%"
  where: Table 2 p8; absolute values Table 8 p21; setup D.2 p19-20

- claim: Three of the nine dataset wins are not statistically significant.
  number: p-value ≪ 0.01 on the other six
  setup: Paired one-tailed t-test; the paper does not say what is paired or how many runs were used.
  quote: "except three datasets (Appetency, Churn and Upselling) the improvements are statistically signiﬁcant with p-value≪ 0.01 measured by the paired one-tailed t-test"
  where: S6 p8

- claim: Stripped to a near-classical GBDT, CatBoost roughly ties the baselines, so the headline lead comes from the added techniques rather than the base implementation.
  number: 0.2% each way on average
  setup: Raw setting: Plain mode, depth 6, no CatBoost categorical options, the same ordered TS permutation for all libraries; 8 datasets (Epsilon absent, no reason given). The main remaining difference is oblivious trees.
  quote: "the raw setting of CatBoost outperforms the baselines in terms of zero-one loss by 0.2% while they are better in terms of logloss by 0.2%"
  where: Table 9 and text, p21-22

- claim: Greedy target statistics cost far more on most datasets than on Adult, and every alternative loses to ordered TS except one Appetency zero-one cell.
  number: Greedy logloss +1.1% on Adult, +40% on Amazon, +57% on Upselling. Leave-one-out +5.5% on Adult, +27% on Internet. Holdout +2.1% on Adult, +8.3% on Amazon.
  setup: TS swapped as options inside CatBoost Ordered mode, "keeping all other algorithmic details the same"; 8 datasets, no Epsilon. Holdout on Appetency zero-one is the exception at -0.5%. A repeat with Plain mode is reported as "very similar" but not shown. This is CatBoost only, not across libraries.
  quote: "Adult +1.1% / +0.8% +2.1% / +2.0% +5.5% / +3.7%" and "Amazon +40% / +32% +8.3% / +8.3% +4.5% / +5.6%" and "Upselling +57% / +50% +1.6% / +0.9% +3.9% / +2.9%"
  where: Table 4 p9

- claim: Ordered mode helps most on small data, but Plain has lower logloss on four of nine datasets.
  number: Plain +1.1% on Adult, +3.9% on Internet; -0.6% on Amazon, -0.05% on Click, -0.06% on Churn, -0.2% on Kick
  setup: Strong setting, Plain relative to Ordered. Authors' explanation: Adult and Internet are "less than 40K training examples". Amazon (32,769 instances, Table 7) is also small and favours Plain, a point the paper does not discuss; that observation is mine.
  quote: "Adult 0.272 (+1.1%) 0.127 (-0.1%)" and "Internet 0.217 (+3.9%) 0.099 (+5.4%)" and "Amazon 0.139 (-0.6%) 0.044 (-1.5%)"
  where: Table 3 and text, p8

- claim: Ordered mode keeps a small average edge in the raw setting, and sharing the permutation between TS and boosting improves it.
  number: Average -0.5% / -0.2% with independent permutations; -0.6% / -0.9% with shared
  setup: Raw setting, relative to Plain, 8 datasets. Amazon logloss is worse in both variants (+0.9%, +0.8%).
  quote: "Average -0.5% / -0.2% -0.6% / -0.9%"
  where: Table 10 p22

- claim: Prediction shift exists formally: reusing one dataset across boosting steps biases the model, and the bias shrinks with n.
  number: bias -(1/(n-1)) c2 (x2 - 1/2), my transcription of garbled text
  setup: Quadratic loss; two i.i.d. Bernoulli(1/2) features; y = c1x1 + c2x2; two stumps; step size 1. Theorem only, for this toy case. Bias "can depend on the relation f∗".
  quote: "we suffer from a bias − 1n−1c2(x2− 12), which is inversely proportional to the data size n"
  where: Theorem 1 p5; proof Appendix A p11-15

- claim: Greedy TS can fit training data perfectly and still predict at chance.
  number: accuracy 0.5
  setup: Thought experiment: all category values unique, P(y=1|category) = 0.5; one split separates training data.
  quote: "the obtained model predicts 0 for all of them ifp<t and predicts 1 otherwise, thus having accuracy 0.5 in both cases"
  where: S3.2 p3

- claim: Leave-one-out does not stop target leakage, because a constant categorical feature still separates the training set perfectly.
  number: none
  setup: Analytic example; threshold depends on n+ and yk.
  quote: "Surprisingly, it does not prevent target leakage."
  where: S3.2 p4

- claim: Ordered TS computes each row's statistic from rows earlier in a random permutation, while test rows use the whole training set.
  number: none
  setup: Meets P1 (no conditional shift) and P2 (uses all data). A single permutation gives early rows high variance, so permutations vary across boosting steps.
  quote: "take Dk ={xj : σ(j) < σ(k)} in Equation (5) for a training example andDk =D for a test one"
  where: S3.2 p4; test handling also S5 p7

- claim: Ordered mode takes about 1.7 times as long per tree as Plain, and XGBoost is slowest in this test.
  number: Plain 1.1 s, Ordered 1.9 s, XGBoost 3.9 s, LightGBM 1.1 s
  setup: Epsilon only (400,000 rows, 2,000 features); fixed-size ensemble of 8,000 trees; depth 6 or 64 leaves; no feature subsampling or bagging; 16 threads, Xeon E3-12xx, 64GB. Time per tree, not time to a given quality.
  quote: "CatBoost Plain 1.1 s" and "CatBoost Ordered 1.9 s" and "XGBoost 3.9 s" and "LightGBM 1.1 s"; "followed by Ordered mode, which is about 1.7 times slower"
  where: C.2 and Table 6, p17-18; S6 p8

- claim: Authors refuse a general speed ranking of libraries.
  number: none
  setup: Their reason is that quality/speed trade-offs differ by library, so only fixed-size training time is reported.
  quote: "one cannot compare libraries by time needed to obtain a certain level of quality"
  where: C.2 p17

- claim: Allowing feature combinations improves logloss, with little gain beyond three features.
  number: 1.86% average (reaching 11.3%) for cmax 2; 2.04% for cmax 3
  setup: Relative to cmax = 1; 8 datasets in Figure 3.
  quote: "changing the number cmax of features allowed to be com-\nbined from 1 to 2 provides an outstanding improvement of logloss by 1.86% (reaching 11.3%),\nchanging from 1 to 3 yields 2.04%"
  where: S6 p9; Appendix G p22

- claim: More permutations help only slightly.
  number: 0.19% at s=3, 0.38% at s=9
  setup: Relative to s=1; average logloss.
  quote: "by 0.19% fors = 3 and by 0.38% fors = 9 compared tos = 1"
  where: S6 p9; p23

- claim: The implementation reduces maintained supporting predictions to linear size, matching standard GBDT with ordered TS asymptotically.
  number: O(sn²) reduced to O(sn)
  setup: Stores models at exponentially spaced prefixes. Compared with other TS types, ordered TS slows some procedures by a factor of s.
  quote: "reduces the number of maintained supporting\npredictions toO(sn )"
  where: S5 p7; proof C.1 p17

- claim: Target statistics need one stored number per category and are the authors' preferred method; one-hot and gradient statistics are out of scope.
  number: none
  setup: Argument, not a benchmark. Relevant to 05b: TS estimate E(y | category), so they require a label.
  quote: "We further focus on ways to calculate TS and leave one-hot encoding and gradient\nstatistics out of the scope of the current paper."
  where: S3.1 p3

LIMITS
- Authors' own benchmark on one random 80/20 split per dataset; tables carry no error bars or spread.
- Baselines never used native categorical handling. LightGBM gradient statistics were excluded from comparison, so the paper does not test CatBoost against library defaults.
- The evaluated models are all scored by logloss and zero-one loss, on tasks using binary metrics. No regression, multiclass or ranking experiments, and no AUC. This is my reading of the tables; the paper states regression targets are supported in principle.
- Theory covers quadratic loss and a toy two-feature case only. "We restrict the rest of Section 4 to this case" (footnote 4, p4).
- Authors concede a bias caveat: "it can also depend on other properties of the dataset" (p8).
- No per-dataset categorical counts or cardinalities (Table 7 gives total features only). No test on temporal data, drift or missing-value strategies; the permutation is "artiﬁcial". 
- Nothing on unsupervised use, clustering, SHAP or interpretability.
- Epsilon is missing from Tables 4, 9, 10 and Figures 2-4 without explanation.
- GPU timing is deferred to GitHub.
- Dated: library versions are from about 2017. Footnote 9 says CatBoost numbers "may slightly differ" from their repository because another version was used, which sits awkwardly with the listed "catboost (0.3)". The "all existing implementations" claim is as of writing.

BUILDS ON
- Friedman 2001 [12] gradient boosting; Friedman 2002 [13] stochastic subsampling; Friedman, Hastie, Tibshirani 2000 [10]; Mason et al. 2000 [24].
- Micci-Barreca 2001 [25] target statistics; Cestnik 1990 [6]; Breiman et al. 1984 [4] and Hastie et al. 2001 [11] for optimal split via TS thresholds.
- O. Zhang 2015 [31] leave-one-out; K. Zhang et al. 2013 [30] conditional shift.
- Breiman 1996 [2] out-of-bag; Breiman 2001 [3] iterated bagging, shown still shifted in Appendix E.
- Online learning inspiration: Bottou and Cun 2004 [1], He et al. 2014 [15], Langford et al. 2009 [18], Ling et al. 2017 [22].
- Oblivious trees: Ferov and Modrý 2016 [9], Gulin et al. 2011 [14], Lou and Obukhov 2017 [23]. Rubin 1981 [28] Bayesian bootstrap.
- Baselines: Chen and Guestrin 2016 [8], Ke et al. 2017 [16].

Raw setting flags, p21: "– – boosting–type Plain – – border–count 255 – – dev–bootstrap–type DiscreteUniform – – gradient–iterations 1 – – random–strength 0 – – depth 6"

FIGURES
- Figure 1, p6, "Ordered boosting principle, examples are ordered according to σ." Shows at a glance that row 7's residual comes from a model trained on rows 1-6.
- Figure 2, p9, "Relative error of Plain boosting mode compared to Ordered boosting mode depending on the fraction of the dataset." Shows Plain worsening as data shrinks across eight datasets; a table would hide that trend.
- Figure 3, p23, "Relative change in logloss for a given allowed complexity compared to the absence of feature combinations." Shows the plateau after 2-3 features, and that one dataset drives the large gain.
- Figure 4, p23, "Relative change in logloss for a given number of permutations s compared to s = 1,". Lower priority; the effect is small.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction flattens maths: superscripts and fractions collapse ("O(1/2n)" is O(1/2^n); "− 1n−1c2(x2− 12)" is -(1/(n-1)) c2 (x2 - 1/2)). Check Theorem 1 against the PDF page before quoting it as a formula.
- Spaces are dropped around symbols ("fors = 3"). Line breaks in quotes shown as \n.
- No embedded instructions found.
- Filename says 2017, matching the arXiv ID; the file itself is v5 from 2019.

Comparison with data-science/01-classical-ml/notes/07-boosting-in-practice.md, for the caller to decide:
- Line 191 says the paper quantifies the TS effect "across libraries". Table 4 compares TS options inside CatBoost only. The figures themselves (1.1%, 40%, 5.5%, 3.9%, 1.7x) match.
- Line 52 says "ahead by 1 to 2%" on Adult, while its own parenthetical and Table 2 give +2.4% and +2.2%. Line 52 also omits that CatBoost additionally had Ordered mode and feature combinations, and that the raw setting loses on Adult (-1.4% / -1.7% logloss for baselines, Table 9).
- data-science/01-classical-ml/notes/05b-clustering-categorical-and-mixed-data.md line 355 is consistent with the paper: TS are defined from the target. The paper says nothing about clustering.
